transcript.content: Hi, welcome in—I'm Dr. [Name]. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, Dr. [Name]. Um, I guess I'm here because my mind just won't stop. It's like I'm constantly jumping from one worry to the next. Lately, I've been obsessing over whether our lab's new partnership is going to mean my position gets cut. And then I start thinking about whether my data are wrong, which leads to worrying about my bills piling up. Then I stress about my family thinking I'm falling behind, and... I don't know, whether I've already completely ruined my chances at getting into grad school. It's just all the time.
How long have you been experiencing this constant worrying across different areas of your life—has it been going on for more than six months, or did it start more recently?

It's been going on for a while now... definitely more than six months. I'd say it's been about seven months. It started right around the time our lab had this big funding shift, and they brought in a commercial partnership. That just changed how everything was being run, and I guess my mind just hasn't stopped spinning since then.
Along with all this worrying, have you noticed physical symptoms like feeling restless or on edge, muscle tension, fatigue, or trouble sleeping nearly every day?

Yeah, definitely. At work, I just feel really wound up... like I can't even settle into my chair. I end up constantly tapping my foot or checking my messages. Sometimes I catch myself just walking back to the instrument room for no actual reason, just because I can't sit still. And I guess I am pretty on edge, because even just normal lab noises have been completely startling me lately.
Would you say your worrying happens even about things that have nothing to do with the lab situation, or does it mostly stay focused on issues connected to that change at work?

It definitely spills over into everything. Um, it's not just the lab. Like I mentioned earlier, it's my bills, my family... everything. I try to stop it, I really do. I'll tell myself to just focus on one task, like finishing a report or checking an assay. But... it just doesn't work. One worry sets off another, and pretty soon I'm just staring at the screen while my head is running through every possible way things could go wrong.

latest_inference.note: Worry has persisted over 7 months, spans multiple unrelated domains (finances, family, career, work), and is accompanied by restlessness, edge, and hypervigilance—meeting core GAD criteria. This pervasiveness beyond the initial work stressor makes adjustment disorder (F43.21) less likely, and the clear symptom pattern rules out the vaguer F41.9.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient reports excessive, difficult-to-control worry spanning multiple life domains (work stability, finances, family perception, academic future) persisting for approximately 7 months, exceeding the 6-month threshold for GAD. Associated symptoms include motor restlessness (foot tapping, inability to sit still, pacing), being easily startled/on edge, and subjective muscle tension. The pervasive, multi-domain nature of the worry (not confined to a single stressor) and chronicity argue against Adjustment Disorder with Anxiety, and there are no reported panic attacks, trauma exposure, obsessions/compulsions, or mood episode features to suggest alternative diagnoses. This presentation fulfills DSM-5-aligned criteria for Generalized Anxiety Disorder (ICD-10 F41.1).
